title: NURS 1017 Unit 5 Case Study 6

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Nurses’ Notes. Highlight the findings that indicate the client is at risk for airway compromise or impaired gas exchange.
question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Highlight these five findings: oriented to person only; hoarse voice with a frequent cough; black-tinged sputum; singed nasal hairs and eyebrows with soot around the nose and mouth; and expiratory wheezes.

Why these findings

  • Hoarse voice and frequent cough: heat and smoke injure the larynx. Swelling there can progress within hours to stridor and complete airway obstruction, so hoarseness is a red-flag cue.
  • Black-tinged (carbonaceous) sputum: soot in the sputum shows that smoke was inhaled below the vocal cords.
  • Singed nasal hairs and eyebrows; soot around the nose and mouth: classic external signs of smoke and heat inhalation, especially after being trapped in an enclosed, smoke-filled room.
  • Expiratory wheezes: bronchospasm and lower-airway irritation from inhaled smoke and chemicals.
  • Oriented to person only: new confusion after smoke exposure suggests cerebral hypoxia from carbon monoxide (CO) and/or impaired gas exchange. It belongs to both Breathing and Disability in the ABCDE sequence.

The headache and nausea in the same note are early signs of CO poisoning, explored in the next question.

Why the other phrases are not airway cues

  • Tearful, asking about his dog: an expected emotional response. He will need support once he is stable.
  • Chest pain 9/10: comes from the partial-thickness (second-degree) burn of the anterior trunk, which is very painful because nerve endings are exposed. It needs treatment, but it is not an airway cue.
  • Circumferential full-thickness burn of the right arm: a circulation concern (risk of compartment syndrome). A circumferential full-thickness burn of the chest could restrict breathing; one of the arm cannot.
  • Ring and watch on the burned arm: they must come off before swelling starts, but they do not signal airway risk.

leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 46-year-old male client brought to the ED after a house fire, with suspected inhalation injury.

question.stem: For each assessment finding, click to specify whether it is consistent with upper airway (inhalation) injury, carbon monoxide poisoning, or hypovolemia related to the burn injury. Each finding may support more than one condition.

rows.text: Hoarse voice
Singed nasal hairs
Headache and nausea
Oriented to person only
SpO2 98% despite new confusion
HR 122 beats/min with BP 104/66 mm Hg
Hematocrit 0.53 L/L (53%)

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 1 — Emergency Department, 0305. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 0305.
question.explanation:
Correct answers

  • Hoarse voice: upper airway (inhalation) injury
  • Singed nasal hairs: upper airway (inhalation) injury
  • Headache and nausea: carbon monoxide poisoning
  • Oriented to person only: upper airway (inhalation) injury and carbon monoxide poisoning
  • SpO2 98% despite new confusion: carbon monoxide poisoning
  • HR 122 beats/min with BP 104/66 mm Hg: hypovolemia related to the burn
  • Hematocrit 0.53 L/L (53%): hypovolemia related to the burn

Why

  • Hoarse voice and singed nasal hairs: direct evidence that hot gas and smoke reached the airway; swelling of the larynx causes the hoarseness.
  • Headache and nausea: early, nonspecific symptoms of CO toxicity. CO binds hemoglobin about 200 times more tightly than oxygen, so less oxygen reaches the tissues.
  • Oriented to person only: both apply. Confusion can come from hypoxemia caused by airway and lung injury, and from tissue hypoxia caused by CO.
  • SpO2 98%: falsely reassuring. A standard pulse oximeter cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin and counts both as saturated. The carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) level on the blood gas drawn at 0320 (pending) is needed.
  • HR 122 beats/min with BP 104/66 mm Hg: burns over 20% TBSA trigger a systemic inflammatory response. Plasma leaks out of the capillaries, intravascular volume falls, and hypovolemic (burn) shock can follow. Tachycardia with a narrowing pulse pressure is compensation. Pain and anxiety contribute, but with a burn this large, volume loss is the main cause.
  • Hematocrit 53%: hemoconcentration. Plasma leaves the vessels while red cells stay, so the hematocrit rises as intravascular volume falls. Hemoglobin and hematocrit are monitored for fluid status.

Beyond the chapter: CO physiology and pulse oximetry are standard content.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client is at highest risk for [[drop0]] as evidenced by [[drop1]]. Once this is addressed, the nurse should next focus on the client's risk for [[drop2]] as evidenced by [[drop3]].

options.text: compartment syndrome of the right arm
airway obstruction from upper airway edema
the hoarse voice and black-tinged sputum
the circumferential full-thickness burn of the right arm
HR 122 beats/min, BP 104/66 mm Hg, and hematocrit 0.53 L/L

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: The client is at highest risk for airway obstruction from upper airway edema as evidenced by the hoarse voice and black-tinged sputum. Once this is addressed, the nurse should next focus on the client's risk for hypovolemic shock as evidenced by HR 122 beats/min, BP 104/66 mm Hg, and hematocrit 0.53 L/L.

Why

  • Airway first: the nurse prioritizes with ABCDE; for burns, airway, breathing and circulation come first, followed by fluid resuscitation. After smoke inhalation, impaired gas exchange takes priority over impaired skin integrity. Upper-airway edema worsens over hours, so recognizing it early allows a controlled intubation before the airway is lost.
  • Circulation next: with about 27% TBSA of partial- and full-thickness burns, large fluid shifts are expected. Tachycardia, a low-normal blood pressure and hemoconcentration show the volume loss; IV access and fluid resuscitation are the top priorities after the airway.

Why the other choices are lower priority

  • Wound infection develops over days, not in the first hours.
  • Hypothermia (Exposure in ABCDE) is a real risk, but it is managed after airway, breathing and circulation.
  • Compartment syndrome of the right arm threatens a limb and needs frequent checks, but a threat to the airway threatens life.
  • Impaired skin integrity, acute pain and disturbed body image are real needs, but none outranks the airway or circulation. Impaired skin integrity is the usual priority for smaller burns; it is displaced when the airway, breathing or circulation is at risk.
  • The other evidence (temperature 36.3° C, WBC 11.2 × 109/L, blistered trunk, pain 9/10, potassium 5.3 mmol/L from cell damage) needs monitoring but does not point to the most urgent risk.

question.stem: The nurse plans the client's fluid resuscitation. Use the Nurses’ Notes (Phase 1), the Rule of Nines, and the provider's orders. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The percentage of TBSA to include in the fluid resuscitation calculation is [[drop0]]. The total volume of Ringer's lactate prescribed for the first 24 hours is [[drop1]]. Half of this volume, [[drop2]], is to be infused over the first 8 hours, timed from [[drop3]]. The nurse will titrate the infusion as prescribed to maintain a urine output of at least [[drop4]].

options.text: the time the IV was started
the time the order was written

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 2 — Emergency Department, 0340. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 0340, the Laboratory Results from 0335, and the Provider Orders from 0340.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: 27%; 8,640 mL; 4,320 mL; timed from 0215 (time of injury); at least 40 mL/h.

Step 1: the percentage of TBSA

  • Anterior trunk (chest and abdomen) 18% + the whole right arm, front 4.5% and back 4.5% = 27%.
  • The face is a superficial (first-degree) burn: red, dry, no blisters. Superficial burns are not counted in resuscitation calculations; adding the face gives the 31.5% distractor, and 18% leaves out the arm.

Step 2: the volumes and the clock

  • 8,640 mL: Parkland formula, 4 mL × 80 kg × 27 = 8,640 mL of Ringer's lactate over 24 hours.
  • 4,320 mL: half is given in the first 8 hours; the other 4,320 mL over the next 16 hours.
  • Timed from 0215: the 8-hour clock starts at the time of the burn, not at arrival, when the IV is started or when the order is written. The first half must be in by 1015; because time has already passed, the hourly rate must make up for it.
  • At least 40 mL/h: the adult target is about 0.5 mL/kg/h (0.5 × 80 kg). Urine output is the key guide for titrating the infusion. Output well above 1 mL/kg/h (for example 100 to 160 mL/h) suggests over-resuscitation, which worsens edema.

Beyond the chapter: the Parkland formula and urine-output targets are standard burn-care practice (Parkland/Baxter; American Burn Association guidance, where current protocols often start at 2 to 4 mL/kg/%TBSA and titrate to urine output). The Rule of Nines is from the chapter.

tabs.title: Provider Orders
tabs.content:
0340:

  • Oxygen 100% via non-rebreather mask until airway secured
  • Ringer's lactate (lactated Ringer's) per Parkland formula: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA (partial- and full-thickness burns only); titrate to urine output
  • Insert indwelling urinary catheter; hourly urine output
  • NPO; nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction
  • Morphine 2–4 mg IV every 1 hour PRN pain
  • Tetanus toxoid IM
  • Chest x-ray; 12-lead ECG
  • Arrange transfer to regional burn centre

leftContent.intro: The nurse is caring for a 46-year-old male client brought to the ED after a house fire, with suspected inhalation injury.

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether it is indicated, contraindicated, or nonessential for the client at this time.

rows.text: Notify the provider immediately about the right-hand findings
Remove the wedding ring and watch from the right hand and wrist
Elevate the right arm on pillows above the level of the heart
Apply a snug elastic compression wrap to the right arm to limit swelling
Continue 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask until the airway is secured
Administer the prescribed morphine intramuscularly into the unburned thigh
Apply ice packs to the blistered chest to relieve pain
Offer small sips of an electrolyte drink to replace fluid losses
Teach active range-of-motion exercises for the right hand
Cover the burns with clean, dry dressings or sheets and keep the room warm

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.explanation:
Correct answers

  • Indicated: notify the provider immediately about the right-hand findings; remove the ring and watch; elevate the right arm above the heart; continue 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask; cover the burns with clean, dry dressings or sheets and keep the room warm.
  • Contraindicated: a snug elastic compression wrap; morphine intramuscularly; ice packs on the chest; sips of an electrolyte drink.
  • Nonessential: teaching active range-of-motion exercises for the right hand.

Why

  • Notify the provider (indicated): cool, pale fingers, capillary refill of 5 seconds, a faint pulse, numbness and tingling, and a tense forearm under a circumferential full-thickness burn signal impending compartment syndrome. The expected treatment is an escharotomy, an incision through the inelastic eschar.
  • Remove the ring and watch (indicated): clothing and jewelry near the burn are removed; once edema develops, a ring or watch acts as a tourniquet.
  • Elevate the arm (indicated): elevation above heart level limits edema formation.
  • Compression wrap (contraindicated): anything constricting raises the compartment pressure that is already compromising perfusion.
  • 100% oxygen (indicated): the COHb of 19% confirms CO poisoning. High-flow oxygen shortens the half-life of carboxyhemoglobin (from about 4 to 6 hours on room air to about 1 to 1½ hours) and continues until the airway is secured and the COHb falls.
  • IM morphine (contraindicated): during burn shock, muscle perfusion is poor, so IM absorption is unreliable: little early relief, then possible delayed, excessive absorption once perfusion returns. Opioids are given IV, as ordered.
  • Ice packs (contraindicated): ice causes vasoconstriction that can deepen the injury, and over a 27% TBSA burn it promotes hypothermia. Burns are cooled with room-temperature water or saline to stop the burning process, not with ice.
  • Electrolyte drink (contraindicated): the client is NPO with a nasogastric tube ordered; intubation is imminent, and large burns commonly cause paralytic ileus. Resuscitation is IV.
  • Range-of-motion teaching (nonessential now): important later, when physical and occupational therapy prevent contractures, but not during an airway emergency with a compromised arm.
  • Clean, dry coverage and a warm room (indicated): protects the wounds from contamination and limits heat loss; hypothermia is a complication of severe burns.

Beyond the chapter: limb elevation, the CO half-life figures and IM absorption in shock are standard content.

question.stem: For each finding on post-injury day 5, click to specify whether it indicates that the plan of care has been effective or not effective.

rows.text: Urine output averaging 55 mL/h over the past 24 hours
Right hand warm, capillary refill 2 seconds, right radial pulse 2+
SpO2 96% on O2 2 L/min nasal cannula; lungs clear; speaks in full sentences
Pain rated 3/10 during a dressing change after IV morphine 30 minutes beforehand
Green-yellow, foul-smelling drainage from the chest wound; redness extending 2 cm beyond the wound edge
Temperature 38.9° C; WBC 17.4 × 10⁹/L

question.footnote: Adapted from OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing (2024), Chapter 14 — Integumentary System (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). This derivative work is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
question.preamble: Phase 3 — Regional Burn Centre, Post-injury Day 5. The nurse has reviewed the Progress Notes from Post-injury Day 5.
question.explanation:
Correct answers

  • Effective: urine output averaging 55 mL/h; right hand warm with capillary refill of 2 seconds and pulse 2+; SpO2 96% on 2 L/min with clear lungs and full sentences; pain 3/10 during the dressing change.
  • Not effective: green-yellow, foul-smelling drainage with redness 2 cm beyond the wound edge; temperature 38.9° C with WBC 17.4 × 109/L.

Why

  • Urine output 55 mL/h: above the 40 mL/h (0.5 mL/kg/h) target, showing adequate renal perfusion after resuscitation.
  • Warm hand, brisk refill, palpable pulse: meets the outcome of no signs of compartment syndrome (no swelling, no decreased pulses) after the escharotomy.
  • SpO2 96%, clear lungs, full sentences: gas exchange and airway patency are restored after extubation.
  • Pain 3/10 during the dressing change: analgesia given at least 30 minutes before burn care keeps pain tolerable before, during and after dressing changes.
  • Purulent, foul drainage with spreading redness: yellow or green, foul-smelling drainage and increasing erythema are signs of burn-wound infection. The nurse notifies the provider (a wound culture and antimicrobials are likely).
  • Fever with WBC 17.4 × 109/L: the goal is a WBC within the normal range. Fever and leukocytosis with a purulent wound suggest infection and possible sepsis, so the nurse escalates promptly.

tabs.content:
0340:

  • Oxygen 100% via non-rebreather mask until airway secured
  • Ringer's lactate (lactated Ringer's) per Parkland formula: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA (partial- and full-thickness burns only); titrate to urine output
  • Insert indwelling urinary catheter; hourly urine output
  • NPO; nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction
  • Morphine 2–4 mg IV every 1 hour PRN pain
  • Tetanus toxoid IM
  • Chest x-ray; 12-lead ECG
  • Arrange transfer to regional burn centre

tabs.title: Progress Notes
tabs.content:
Post-injury Day 5:Right-arm escharotomy was performed on arrival at the burn centre. Client was extubated on day 3. Morphine IV given 30 minutes before each dressing change. Silver sulfadiazine and nonadherent dressings applied to the anterior trunk twice daily. Today's assessment findings are shown below.

Urine output averaging 55 mL/h over the past 24 hours. Right hand warm, capillary refill 2 seconds, right radial pulse 2+. SpO2 96% on O2 2 L/min nasal cannula; lungs clear; speaks in full sentences. Pain rated 3/10 during a dressing change after IV morphine 30 minutes beforehand. Green-yellow, foul-smelling drainage from the chest wound; redness extending 2 cm beyond the wound edge. Temperature 38.9° C; WBC 17.4 × 10⁹/L.
